prompt: What does RAG stand for, and what are the two main steps in the process it describes?
keyPoints: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Step 1: retrieve documents relevant to the user's question
Step 2: give those documents to the LLM as context so it generates the answer from them
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Q1)

prompt: RAG is often pitched as a fix for two specific LLM problems. Name them, and for each explain why *retrieval* helps (not just why the problem exists).
keyPoints: Stale knowledge: models are frozen at a training cutoff; retrieval supplies current information at answer time
Hallucination: models guess to fill gaps (private or missing data); retrieved text gives them something real to ground the answer in
Mechanism: the relevant text sits in the prompt at the moment of answering, so the model doesn't rely on frozen weights alone
Bonus: grounding makes answers traceable to a source
pitfalls: Explaining why the problems exist (cutoffs, missing private data) but skipping how retrieval fixes them
Hallucination side is the thin one: needs the 'grounding instead of guessing' idea
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Q2, needed a hint)

prompt: RAG is often described with an open-book exam analogy. Who is the student, what is the book, and where does the analogy break down?
keyPoints: Student = the LLM; book = the document collection
Breakdown: the LLM never flips through the book. A separate component (embedding model + vector search) finds the pages and hands them over
Retrieval is its own stage before generation, so bad retrieval means a bad answer however good the LLM is (garbage in, garbage out)
pitfalls: Treating the LLM as the thing that searches the documents
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Q3, needed a hint)

prompt: Name three real-world RAG applications and, for each, say what the knowledge source is that gets retrieved from.
keyPoints: Three distinct, plausible applications (e.g. support assistants, code or UI generation, document Q&A, internal knowledge search)
Each paired with a concrete source: FAQ/help-center articles, a component or code library, a chunked and embedded document library
Mentions that sources get chunked and embedded so they can be searched by meaning
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Q4, solid first try)

prompt: Why does chunking matter in a RAG pipeline? What goes wrong if chunks are too big, and what goes wrong if they are too small?
keyPoints: Chunking decides what a 'page' looks like to the retriever: the unit that gets embedded, searched and handed to the LLM
Too big: a chunk covers several ideas so its embedding is a muddy average, and it wastes context window on irrelevant text
Too small: a chunk loses surrounding context, so it may match well but not contain enough to answer
Chunking is part of retrieval quality, not a formatting detail
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Claude's nudge after Q4)

prompt: Even with retrieval, a RAG system can still give a wrong or made-up answer. Name two distinct ways that happens.
keyPoints: Retrieval failure: the retrieved chunks are irrelevant, weakly relevant or missing the answer, and the LLM still writes a fluent, confident answer from mediocre context
Generation failure: the right content was retrieved but the model ignores, misreads or over-extends it
Other valid modes: chunk boundaries cut the answer in half, conflicting or outdated documents, a similarity threshold that is too loose
Takeaway: failures look plausible, which is why you inspect the retrieved chunks first when debugging
source: Extension of RAG quiz Q3 and the vector-similarity code review (fluent answers from mediocre context)

prompt: Your document library supports keyword search ('Africa' returns documents with 'Africa' in the title) but can't answer natural-language questions. Sketch the RAG design: what gets stored, what happens when a user asks a question, and what the user gets back.
keyPoints: Ingest: split documents into chunks, embed each chunk with an embedding model, store vectors plus metadata (source, title) in a vector store
Query time: embed the question with the same model, find the top-k most similar chunks
Generation: pass the question and retrieved chunks to an LLM, which writes the answer
Output: a summary plus the sources it came from
Why keyword search fails: it matches literal words, not meaning
pitfalls: Using a different embedding model for the query than for the documents
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Q4, Tom's own use case)

prompt: What does 'fine-tuning' mean in machine learning, and how does it differ from prompt engineering and from RAG? Think about what happens to the model itself in each case.
keyPoints: Fine-tuning = continuing a pretrained model's training on your own dataset, so its weights change; the result is a new version of the model
Prompt engineering / API settings: the model is unchanged, you steer it with instructions or parameters at call time
RAG: the model is unchanged, you supply documents at call time
Fine-tuning is not changing the model choice, the prompt or the config values
pitfalls: Equating fine-tuning with prompt engineering or tweaking API configuration
If he doesn't know a term, he should say so and ask for the definition rather than reasoning around it
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Q5, needed the definition from Claude)

prompt: Give one scenario where fine-tuning beats RAG, and one where RAG beats fine-tuning. Say why in each case.
keyPoints: Fine-tuning wins for a skill or behavior gap: consistent tone, structure or format, specialized behavior long prompts can't reliably produce; can also shorten prompts at scale
RAG wins for a knowledge gap: facts that change often, private data, or when answers need citations
Fine-tuning is a poor way to teach facts and can't say where an answer came from
They're complementary, and fine-tuning is usually the last resort because it is expensive
pitfalls: Giving a general opinion instead of one concrete scenario for each side
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Q5)

prompt: A RAG system is giving poor answers. How do you work out whether it's a retrieval problem or a generation problem, and what would you change in each case?
keyPoints: Look at the retrieved chunks first, before touching the model
Wrong or irrelevant chunks = retrieval problem: change chunking, the embedding model, the search strategy or the similarity threshold
Right chunks but a poor answer = generation problem: change the prompt, the model or the call settings
Fine-tuning only comes in later, if the model lacks the skill even with good context and good prompting
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 1 (Tom's own diagnostic split in Q5)

prompt: What does a cosine similarity of 1.0 mean? What would 0 tell you, and what about -1?
keyPoints: 1.0: the vectors point in the same direction (maximally similar in direction)
0: orthogonal, no directional relationship
-1: opposite directions
Cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between the vectors, not the angle itself
pitfalls: Saying the score 'is the angle'
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 2 (Q1) and a correction during the code review

prompt: Define dot product and cosine similarity, and explain how the two are related.
keyPoints: Dot product: multiply matching coordinates and sum them
Cosine similarity: the dot product divided by the product of the two vectors' magnitudes, which equals the dot product of the normalized vectors
dot(a, b) = |a| x |b| x cos(angle), so the dot product mixes direction with magnitude and cosine isolates direction
For vectors already normalized to length 1, the two are identical
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 2 and the vector-similarity code review

prompt: Why do we normally prefer cosine similarity over a raw dot product for text embeddings? Can you think of a case where magnitude carries real signal?
keyPoints: Cosine ignores magnitude, so vector length doesn't swamp the ranking when you only care about meaning (direction)
Cosine is bounded to [-1, 1], so a threshold like 0.7 means the same thing across queries and datasets
Normalizing discards magnitude on purpose
Magnitude can carry real signal in some systems, e.g. recommendations where it reflects popularity or strength of engagement
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 2

prompt: Why do texts with similar meaning end up as nearby vectors? What in the way an embedding model is trained makes that happen?
keyPoints: Embedding models are trained with a contrastive objective: pull the vectors of related text pairs together and push unrelated pairs apart
Nearness in the space therefore reflects meaning, because that is what the training rewarded
It is not RLHF (that is for shaping chat behavior from human preference)
Similar meaning does not require shared words, which is why this beats keyword search
pitfalls: Naming RLHF or 'the LLM just understands' as the reason
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 2

prompt: Write two sentences you'd expect to score about 0.9 under cosine similarity with a typical text embedding model, and two you'd expect to score close to 0.1. Why those?
keyPoints: High pair: same meaning in different words (paraphrases), e.g. 'The cat sat on the mat' / 'A feline rested on the rug'
Low pair: unrelated topics, e.g. a sentence about tax deadlines and one about volcanoes
Similarity tracks meaning, not shared words
Exact numbers depend on the model; unrelated text often doesn't score near zero or below, so thresholds need calibrating per model
source: RAG fundamentals quiz, session 2 (Tom's own quiz prompt)

prompt: An embedding has hundreds of dimensions. Is each dimension a labeled feature like 'royalty' or 'gender'? Explain what a dimension is and where the meaning actually lives.
keyPoints: No: dimensions are learned coordinates, not labeled slots
A vector is one point, and the number of dimensions is its length, i.e. how many coordinates it has
Meaning lives in directions and patterns across many dimensions, not in any single one
Careful with terms: 'vector' (the point) vs 'dimension' (one coordinate/axis)
pitfalls: Treating each dimension as a human-readable property
Using 'vectors' and 'dimensions' interchangeably
source: Word-math video script session (dimensions treated as labeled slots)

prompt: Explain king - man + woman ~ queen using the 'map and pins' picture: what is a vector, what is the arithmetic doing, and what actually finds 'queen'?
keyPoints: A vector is a spot on the map; each word is a pin
The arithmetic is a walk: start at 'king', apply the male-to-female step, and land on a spot that probably has no pin
Nearest-neighbor search with cosine similarity finds the closest pin, which is 'queen'
It's evidence the space has meaningful geometry: directions like male-to-female exist
source: Word-math video script session

prompt: In RAG, what plays the role of the 'spot you land on' and what plays the role of 'queen'? What step does RAG skip compared with word math?
keyPoints: The query's embedding is the spot you land on
Document chunks are the pins; the top-k nearest chunks are the 'queen' you find near the spot
RAG skips the arithmetic walk: the embedding model places the query on the map directly
Shared step: nearest-neighbor search by cosine similarity, and what matters is the ranking, not near vs far
pitfalls: Swapping the labels: calling the query the pin you find, or saying both vectors are 'a walk'
source: Word-math video script session (needed explanation to click)

prompt:
Here is the pipeline inside `findTopSimilarDocuments`:

```ts
documents
  .map((d) => ({ document: d, similarity: cosineSimilarity(queryVector, d.embedding) }))
  .filter((d) => d.similarity >= minSimilarity)
  .sort((a, b) => b.similarity - a.similarity)
  .slice(0, topK);
```

Why must `sort` come before `slice`? What would happen if you sliced first, and would anything throw?
keyPoints: slice takes the first K by position, so only after a descending sort are the first K the best K
Slicing first keeps K arbitrary items (input order) and then sorts just those, so the best documents can be dropped
Nothing throws: the output is plausible but silently wrong
Filtering before sorting is just cheaper; the real correctness constraint is sort-before-slice
pitfalls: Naming filter-before-slice as the key ordering constraint instead of sort-before-slice
source: Vector-similarity code review (slice-before-sort is the actual bug)

prompt: Someone writes the comparator as `(a, b) => a.similarity - b.similarity` in the same pipeline. What does the function now return, and why is this kind of bug hard to catch?
keyPoints: That sorts ascending, so `slice(0, topK)` returns the K least similar documents that passed the filter
No error is thrown and the results all look 'above threshold', so the output seems reasonable
In RAG the LLM then writes a fluent answer from weak context, so the failure shows up as subtly worse answers
Catch it with a test that asserts the first result has the highest similarity
source: Vector-similarity code review

prompt: Someone swaps `cosineSimilarity` for a raw `dotProduct` in the map step, on vectors that are not normalized, and leaves `minSimilarity = 0.7` alone. What goes wrong, and does the ranking stay the same?
keyPoints: Dot product scores are unbounded and depend on vector magnitudes, so 0.7 no longer means 'reasonably similar'
With large vectors nearly everything passes; with small vectors good matches fall below 0.7 and the list can come back empty
Ranking changes too: dot = |q| x |d| x cos(angle). |q| is the same for every document, but |d| varies, so long vectors can outrank better directional matches
'The sort works correctly' only means it orders the scores correctly, not that it ranks like cosine would
With pre-normalized vectors, dot product and cosine are identical
pitfalls: Concluding the top-K would be the same because sort and slice still work mechanically
source: Vector-similarity code review (got the first half, missed the ranking change)

prompt: What does `findTopSimilarDocuments` do if a document's embedding has a different length than the query vector, say 768 vs 512 dimensions? Reason through the plausible behaviors of the similarity helper and say which are dangerous.
keyPoints: Depends on the helper: it may throw (loud, good), or silently ignore the extra dimensions or produce NaN (dangerous)
A silently wrong score looks like any other score, so bad documents can rank high or good ones vanish with no error
Root cause is usually mixing embeddings from different models, whose spaces aren't comparable even at equal length
Fix: validate lengths match and fail loudly, and store the embedding model's id with each vector
source: Vector-similarity code review (Q4, parked and never answered)

prompt: The `minSimilarity` filter can leave you with an empty array. What should the system do then, and why is the threshold a floor rather than a quality guarantee?
keyPoints: Handle the empty case explicitly: tell the user nothing relevant was found, or fall back to something else, rather than calling the LLM with no or weak context
Everything above 0.7 is weakly relevant at best, not necessarily good
The LLM will write a fluent, confident answer from mediocre context, so the failure looks plausible
'Irrelevant' overstates what low-scoring documents are: the risk is in the weakly relevant ones that pass
pitfalls: Calling the documents that pass the threshold 'irrelevant' or calling the threshold a guarantee
source: Vector-similarity code review (Q2)

prompt: `findTopSimilarDocuments` scores and sorts every document on every query. What does that cost, and how do production systems like Pinecone avoid it?
keyPoints: Scoring every document is O(n x d) per query, and a full sort adds O(n log n)
Cheaper exact top-k: keep a heap of size k, O(n log k) instead of sorting everything
At scale, vector databases use approximate nearest neighbor indexes such as HNSW (graph-based) to avoid scanning everything
Trade-off: a small loss in recall for a large gain in speed
source: Vector-similarity code review (performance tradeoffs)

prompt: In your own words, define each of these in one sentence: vector, embedding, dimension, embedding model, vector search. Say how they relate.
keyPoints: Vector: an ordered list of numbers, a point (or direction) in space
Embedding: a vector that represents the meaning of a piece of text, produced by an embedding model
Dimension: one coordinate or axis; the count is the length of the vector
Embedding model: the neural network that maps text to vectors
Vector search: finding the stored vectors nearest to a query vector
pitfalls: Using 'vector' and 'dimension' loosely or interchangeably
Guessing instead of saying 'I don't know this term'
source: Pattern across the RAG tutoring chats (imprecise terminology)

prompt: Your RAG app embeds a question, finds the three closest chunks and shows them to the user. Is that RAG? What is missing, and what does the user get in a full RAG system?
keyPoints: Retrieval alone is semantic (vector) search: it returns the matching chunks as a ranked list of results
RAG adds generation: the question and the retrieved chunks are put into the LLM's prompt as context
The LLM writes an answer grounded in those chunks, so the user gets an answer (ideally with sources) instead of a list of passages to read
Retrieval quality still caps answer quality: if the wrong chunks come back, the LLM works from the wrong context
pitfalls: Ending the description of RAG at 'return the closest chunks to the user' and skipping the LLM step
source: Word-math video review (the video's RAG section stopped at 'return them to the user')

prompt: king - man + woman lands near 'queen' but not exactly on it. Give two reasons it isn't exact, and say how far you'd trust the trick as a general rule about embeddings.
keyPoints: The male-to-female step is not one perfectly clean arrow, so the walk doesn't land exactly on any word's spot
A word's position reflects how the word is used in text, not its real-world meaning: 'queen' also appears around the band, chess and so on, which pulls it away from the clean royal-female spot
The result is a point with no pin on it, so you take the nearest word by cosine similarity, and a similarity of exactly 1.0 is essentially never reached

The trick comes from older word-embedding models such as word2vec and works approximately, on well-chosen examples. Demos typically exclude the input words, because the nearest word is often one of the inputs (e.g. 'king' itself)
It is evidence that the space has meaningful directions, not a description of how RAG retrieves
pitfalls: Saying 'most likely the closest point is queen' without hedging
Explaining the gap as queen having less status or power than king (a real-world claim) instead of how the word is used in text
source: Word-math video script session and the video review

prompt: On the 'map and pins' picture, what does 'closest pin' actually mean when you use cosine similarity? How is that different from straight-line (Euclidean) distance, and when would the two give the same ranking?
keyPoints: Cosine similarity compares the angle between two arrows drawn from the center of the map; it ignores how long the arrows are
Euclidean distance is the straight-line gap between the two points, so it is sensitive to vector length as well as direction
Two vectors can point the same way (cosine 1.0) while being far apart as points, if one is much longer
For vectors normalized to length 1, squared Euclidean distance = 2 - 2 x cosine similarity, so both metrics give the same ranking
So 'closest' must always be said with its measure: closest in angle, or closest in distance
pitfalls: Saying 'closest points' without saying how closeness is measured
source: Word-math video review (the video says 'closest point' four times and never defines it)

prompt: You're given an embedding model and need to pick a similarity function for your vector index. What is the general rule, and when is the choice between cosine and dot product irrelevant?
keyPoints: Rule of thumb: use the same similarity function the model was trained with, because that is the score its vectors were shaped to make meaningful (check the model card or docs)
Some models only specify dot product as a suitable score, so cosine wouldn't be the right choice for them
If the model was trained with cosine, you can use cosine, or normalize and use dot product: the two are mathematically equivalent
Where magnitude carries real signal (e.g. popularity in a recommender), dot product keeps it and cosine throws it away
If you don't know what the model was trained with, test candidate metrics on your own data
pitfalls: Describing dot product as being for 'multiple elements within a document' instead of as a score that uses vector length as a signal
Not mentioning that with pre-normalized vectors the choice makes no difference
source: Vector-similarity session Q4 (Tom's research from the Pinecone 'Vector Similarity Explained' article)

prompt: A colleague proposes: normalize every vector once when it is stored, then use plain dot product at search time. Why does that give cosine-similarity results more cheaply, what must you do to the query, and when is it the wrong move?
keyPoints: Normalizing divides each vector by its length, so every vector has length 1 and only direction survives. Cosine then equals the dot product, which skips the magnitude calculation on every comparison
It is done once per stored vector at write time, a small cost next to embedding the text, while the savings repeat on every query against millions of vectors

Normalize the query too. If only the stored vectors are unit length, the ranking is unchanged (the query's length scales every score equally) but the scores are no longer bounded to [-1, 1], so a threshold like 0.7 stops meaning the same thing
Normalizing discards magnitude for good and nothing factors it back in. Fine when magnitude is noise (typical for text), wrong when it carries signal, e.g. popularity
Many models output already-normalized vectors, in which case there is nothing to do
pitfalls: Wondering whether normalizing loses magnitude or whether the magnitude is later factored back in (it is lost, and cosine ignores it anyway)
Normalizing only the stored vectors and leaving the query raw
source: Vector-similarity session Q4 follow-ups (Tom's normalize-at-index-time reasoning)
